text: This foil triangle flies.
Nothing on it moves.
No wings. No rotor. No fuel.
So is it antigravity?
Take it apart.
Nineteen twenty-eight. A British patent.
Three parts.
About thirty thousand volts go across them.
The sharp wire's field ionises the air.
Ions race to the foil, bumping into air.
Each bump passes on a push. A wind.
The wind blows down. The lifter goes up.
Not antigravity. Ion wind.
A real plane has flown on it.
Twenty eighteen. No moving parts. About sixty metres, the length of a gym.
Stillwing asks: what if you stacked them?
Thirty kilovolts per cell. Zero moving parts.
Trial one: a foil cell lifts its own three grams.
Trial two: sixty-four cells carry two kilos.
Trial three: twelve hundred cells. A full wing.
The wing flies twelve kilometres, on its own batteries. Silent.
One catch.
It pushes on air.
Up high, the air thins. So does the thrust.
It stalls out at three kilometres.
In the vacuum chamber: zero.
Stillwing is cleared.
Below three kilometres.
Not as antigravity.
Just wire, foil, and air.
Case closed. The next file opens Sunday.
